A B S T R A C T
Thousands of ancient agricultural terraced ﬁelds exist in ephemeral stream valleys in the central Negev desert.
Their stone terrace walls captured runoﬀwater, ﬂowing from the surrounding hillslope catchments, to increase
moisture in the loess soils of the terraced ﬁelds. Geoarchaeological research at the site of Horvat Haluqim
discovered evidence for ancient farming and soil manuring in this arid desert region during various archae-
ological periods. Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and Digital Elevation Models (DEM) enable the devel-
opment of hydrological models to investigate every ancient terraced ﬁeld in a non-invasive manner, without
disturbing the archaeological remains. We developed a GIS-based hydrological model, coupled with the D-
Inﬁnity (Tau DEM) algorithm, to evaluate annual runoﬀyields in 13 ancient terraced ﬁelds at the rural ar-
chaeological site of Horvat Haluqim. Our model precisely determined the runoﬀcatchment area, ranging be-
tween 0.10 ha and 0.36 ha, of each individual terraced ﬁeld. Supervised land cover classiﬁcation, using Erdas
Imagine, showed the surface percentages of crusted loess soil and exposed bedrock. Following an evaluation of
runoﬀcoeﬃcients established by conventional hydrological studies in the region, we present results of model-
calculated runoﬀoverland ﬂow yields. We modelled runoﬀamounts for each of the agricultural ﬁelds during an
average year (1989–90) with 88 mm precipitation, a very wet year (1991–92) with 188 mm, and a severe
drought year (1999–2000) with only 34 mm rainfall. Our initial results, based on an approximated average
annual runoﬀcoeﬃcient of 10%, indicate that runoﬀwater amounts during an average and wet rainfall year
appear suﬃcient to grow agricultural crops in these ancient ﬁelds. However, drought years are of course more
problematic. The modelling results are supported by the successful growth of trees in similar terraced wadi ﬁelds
next to Horvat Haluqim, established by the Jewish National Fund. Given the inherent uncertainties involved in
modelling, it is encouraging to note that the trees did survive also drought years. Our model may be applied to
evaluate the eﬀect of climatic changes on runoﬀwater harvesting systems, looking back into the past and also to
assess possible impact of future climate change scenarios in modern water harvesting projects.
1. Introduction
The average annual precipitation in the Negev Highlands at present
is approximately 100 mm and the average annual evaporation from a
class A pan is about 2600 mm (Goldreich, 2003). Therefore, rainfall
amounts are obviously insuﬃcient for dry farming, whether for the
production of seasonal food grains (barley, wheat), or perennial trees.
Nevertheless, thousands of stone terrace walls exist in ephemeral dry
stream valleys (wadi in Arabic, nahal in Hebrew) of the central Negev
Highlands (Fig. 1). These terrace walls were built in ancient times to
capture runoﬀrainwater, so that soil moisture is increased considerably
in the terraced agricultural ﬁelds. Widespread crusted loess soils en-
abled agriculture in this arid desert region, both in the generation of
runoﬀon the slopes and also in the preservation of captured runoﬀ
water in the loess soils of the terraced agricultural ﬁelds (Evenari et al.,
1982; Shanan and Schick, 1980; Bruins, 1986, 1990; 2012; Ore and
Bruins, 2012).
The excavations of ancient terraced ﬁelds at the rural archaeological
site of Horvat Haluqim (Bruins et al., 1986; 2012; Bruins and Van der
Plicht, 2017a, 2017b) (Fig. 1) show that stone terrace walls were built
in stream channels, which already contained alluvial loess soils. These
soils have a silt-loam texture with an excellent water-holding capacity,

The stone terrace walls were ﬁrst and foremost built to harvest runoﬀ
water, but the eﬀect of water capture and the slowing down of the ﬂow
of water also induced aggradation of ﬁne loessial sediment transported
by the runoﬀfrom the hillslope catchments during rainfall events. The
gradual soil aggradation on the terraced ﬁelds was a distinct additional
beneﬁt of runoﬀwater harvesting, leading also to soil harvesting, re-
sulting in increasing soil depth. Shanan (2000) measured the amount of
sediment transported from the hillslopes by runoﬀﬂows at the re-
constructed ancient Avdat Farm (Fig. 1), dated to the Byzantine period
(324–640 CE). The pre-farming environment with regard to sediments

The areal extent of ancient terraced ﬁelds in the region was ﬁrst
surveyed by Kedar (1967), using aerial photographs. The most recent
update and evaluation of the spatial distribution of ancient terrace walls
in the Negev (Fig. 1) was carried out by Bruins (2012) in relation to a
new climatic classiﬁcation of southern Israel, based on the P/PET index
(P = annual precipitation, PET = potential annual evapotranspiration).
Most ancient agricultural terrace walls are situated in the Arid Zone, in
between the P/PET range of 0.05 and 0.10. Dry farming, based on di-
rect rainfall, is only viable, according to UNEP (1997), in the Semi-Arid
Zone and wetter regions, having a P/PET index above 0.20. Therefore,
additional water is/was clearly necessary to facilitate agriculture in the
central Negev Highlands.
A simple classiﬁcation system, based on farm design in terms of
runoﬀ/ﬂoodwater supply was described by Bruins et al. (1986), in
which three ancient systems are deﬁned: (1) Terraced Wadi System; (2)
Hillside Conduit System; and (3) Diversion System. The latter has the
most extensive landscape coverage, involving large wadis from which
ﬂoodwater is captured by diversion channels. The diverted ﬂoodwater
is subsequently conducted to terraced ﬁelds, situated in the adjacent
alluvial valley.
The Terraced Wadi System is probably the oldest and most common
in the Negev Highlands (Bruins, 2012), characterised by a series of
stone terrace walls in the wadi bed (Ore and Bruins, 2012), without any
conduit or diversion channels. Each terraced ﬁeld in this system, par-
ticularly in wadis of low stream order, receives runoﬀoverland ﬂow
mainly from the adjacent hillslopes. Our paper is focussed on this
system, as presented here in relation to the rural archaeological site of
Horvat Haluqim, characterised by terraced wadis of the 1st stream
order.
Concerning the chronological span of ancient runoﬀ-capturing ter-
raced ﬁelds, the oldest stone wall barrage systems (i.e. terraced wadi),
dated to the 7th millennium BCE (Pre-Pottery Neolithic B), is situated in
the desert of south-east Jordan (Fuji, 2007; Bruins, 2012). The oldest
evidence in the central Negev Highlands for terraced wadi ﬁelds has
been found by Bruins (2012) at Horvat Haluqim, dated by radiocarbon
to about 5000–4700 cal BCE. Other periods found at Horvat Haluqim in
relation to terraced wadi ﬁelds, dated by radiocarbon (Bruins, 2012;
Bruins et al., 2012, 2018; Bruins and Van der Plicht, 2017a, 2017b), are
the Late Bronze Age (ca 1550–1200 BCE), Iron Age I (ca 1200–980
BCE), Iron Age II (ca 980–586 BCE), Persian period (539–332 BCE),
Roman period (37 BCE–324 CE), and Early Islamic period (640–1099
BCE). Various soil layers in the terraced wadi ﬁelds at Horvat Haluqim
show unmistakable evidence of manuring by ash from kitchen ﬁres
(also containing pieces of animal bones and broken pottery) and from
animal dung (Bruins, 2012; Bruins and Jongmans, 2012; Bruins and
Van der Plicht, 2017a, 2017b). Agricultural development in other ter-
raced wadi ﬁelds in the Negev during the Byzantine and Early Islamic
periods has been studied by Avni et al. (2013), using OSL dating.
The Hillside Conduit System, probably developed during the
Byzantine period, is characterised by terraced wadi ﬁelds that receive
runoﬀmainly as channel ﬂow through conduits built on the adjacent
hillslopes, which capture the runoﬀoverland ﬂow and convert it to
channel ﬂow. The latter type of ﬂow is much faster than overland ﬂow.
Thus signiﬁcantly more runoﬀwater can be harvested from the ad-
jacent hillslopes and conducted unto the agricultural terraced ﬁelds in
the valley (Shanan and Schick, 1980; Evenari et al., 1982; Bruins et al.,
1986).
There are hundreds of ancient farming units with numerous stone
terrace walls in the Negev Highlands (Evenari et al., 1958; Kedar, 1967;
Ashkenazi et al., 2012). So far only two ancient farming units, near
Shivta and near Avdat (Fig. 1), were reconstructed and investigated in a
detailed manner in terms of hydrology and agronomy, using rain gauges
and hydrographs to measure the amount of rainfall and resulting runoﬀ
ﬂowing unto the terraced ﬁelds (Evenari et al., 1982; Shanan and
Schick, 1980; Shanan, 2000). Both investigated farming units belong to
the Hillside Conduit System.
It is clearly impossible, besides being very costly and labour-in-
tensive, to investigate each and every ancient agricultural ﬁeld with
hydrographs, conventional hydrological ﬁeldwork and agricultural
ﬁeld trials. Moreover, such invasive research is bound to eradicate and
alter the original archaeological soil record and related building re-
mains.
As an alternative, Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and Digital
Elevation Models (DEM) do enable the development of non-invasive
detailed investigation of virtually each and every ancient agricultural
terraced ﬁeld in the Negev. An earlier GIS-based hydrological model,
developed by the third author (Svoray, 2004), was applied to assess
runoﬀcontribution at Horvat Benayah, a semi-arid area with wadi
terraces south of Hebron (Ackermann et al., 2008).
We have further developed the Svoray (2004) and Ackermann et al.
(2008) models, coupled with the D-Inﬁnity (Tau DEM) algorithm
(Tarboton, 1997), to assess runoﬀyields at the rural archaeological site
of Horvat Haluqim in the central Negev desert, near Kibbutz Sede Boker
(Fig. 1). The Terraced Wadi System, which has not been investigated so
far in terms of runoﬀyields by individual terraced ﬁelds, is present at
this site. Here we show results of model-calculated runoﬀoverland ﬂow
yields in 13 ancient terraced ﬁelds at Horvat Haluqim during an
average year (1989–90) with 88 mm precipitation, a very wet year
(1991–92) with 188 mm, and a severe drought year (1999–2000) with
only 34 mm rainfall.
Dealing with ancient agriculture in the central Negev Highlands, a
concise background is given of palaeoclimate during the Holocene and
the range of climatic ﬂuctuations, also including modern times. The
past climate in the southern Levant during the Holocene is reﬂected by
lake level changes of the Dead Sea, which can be considered as a large
regional rain gauge.
The largest ephemeral stream in the central Negev Highlands, Nahal
Zin, having a catchment of 1400 km2, ﬂows to the Dead Sea (Fig. 1).
The palaeo-hydrology of Nahal Zin was investigated by Greenbaum
et al. (2000) along a canyon near the Arava valley (Fig. 1), based on
slackwater deposits and other sedimentary indicators. The authors also
studied the occurrence of ﬂoods in Nahal Zin during modern times in
relation to instrumental and historical records. They presented evidence
of 28 large ﬂoods in Nahal Zin during the past 2000 years, ranging in
magnitude from 200 to 1500 m3 per second. A good correlation exists
between high Dead Sea levels, indicating a comparatively wetter cli-
mate, and a high frequency of large ﬂood events during the period
620–1120 CE and during the modern period 1940–2000. Periods with
low ﬂood frequency (270–620 CE and 1120–1940 CE) correlate with
low Dead Sea levels, indicating a drier climate. The authors also note
that the period 1120–1470 CE is characterised by a small number of
very large ﬂoods. The respective eﬀects of either Mediterranean or Red
Sea meteorological depression systems on the Nahal Zin catchment are
factors to be considered. Modern instrumental data available since
1935 show a positive relation between Dead Sea levels and rainfall

Other studies include an exceptional high lake level of −372 m, dated

not move southward into the central Negev, which remained arid
(Bruins, 2012). The variability of the average climate, say for periods of
30 years, will show much less change in terms of rainfall amounts than
the annual variations. Proxy palaeoclimatic indicators usually reﬂect a
multi-year average. Given the range of Holocene lake level variations in
the Dead Sea (Bookman et al., 2004), as compared to Dead Sea levels
during the 19th and 20th centuries, before water pumping from the

In fact, during severe drought years, such as 1998–1999 and

Negev and the Arava Rift Valley (Fig. 1), penetrated not only into the
central Negev, but also into the northern Negev, while most of Israel

almost the entire country of Israel is under a desert climate (Kaﬂe and

In conclusion, the above proxy palaeoclimatic indicators and
modern instrumental data of annual climatic ﬂuctuations suggest that
climatic conditions in the central Negev were usually arid during
average rainfall years and wet years, but hyper-arid during drought
years. Therefore, additional runoﬀwater in the region was necessary to
enable agriculture during diﬀerent archaeological periods (Bruins,
2012). Moreover, farming by a settled population in the central Negev
desert is not necessarily related to wetter climatic periods. Political and
human factors also played an important role that determined perma-
nent settlement and runoﬀfarming, even during comparatively dry
phases such as the Byzantine and Early Islamic periods (Bruins, 1994;
Avni et al., 2013; Fuks et al., 2017).
2. Objectives and methodology
As aforementioned, it is diﬃcult to investigate each and every an-
cient agricultural ﬁeld in the Negev desert with hydrographs, conven-
tional hydrological ﬁeldwork and agricultural ﬁeld trials. The remark-
able development of GIS and DEMs during the past decades enables
new research methodologies that facilitate non-invasive detailed in-
vestigation of each ancient agricultural system and terraced ﬁeld in the
Negev.
We focus here on a 1st order terraced wadi at the rural archae-
ological site of Horvat Haluqim (Cohen, 1976; Bruins et al., 1986;
Bruins and Ore, 2008; Bruins et al., 2012; Bruins and Van der Plicht,
2017a, 2017b), located 1.7 km north-east of Kibbutz Sede Boker in the
central Negev desert (Figs. 1 and 2). Agricultural ﬁelds in Terraced
Wadi Systems of low order stream channels are situated in the upper
reaches of the watershed (Fig. 2). Therefore, the terraced wadi ﬁelds
receive mainly runoﬀwater from the adjacent hillslopes as overland
ﬂow. Most rainfall events in the region are in the range of 3–10 mm
(Sharon, 1972; Evenari et al., 1982). Such mild to moderate rainfalls in
the small watersheds at Horvat Haluqim cause overland ﬂow along the
hillslopes, being about 40–80 m in length, as witnessed by the ﬁrst
author during various rainfall events. Even if channel ﬂow develops in
the wadi bed (ﬂoodwater), the ﬂows are gentle.
A nearby modern terraced wadi system (1st order stream channel),
built by the Jewish National Fund to establish trees in the desert, shows

so far not been investigated in terms of runoﬀamounts received by
individual terraced ﬁelds. For example, investigating runoﬀyields by

conventional hydrology would require 26 landscape changes along the
lowermost part of the slope just above each ﬁeld and installation of 26

3. Runoﬀcoeﬃcients in the central Negev desert
We evaluated runoﬀcoeﬃcients measured by hydrological research
in the central Negev region and the factors involved. Such an evaluation
is necessary to present the rational concerning our selection of an
average annual runoﬀcoeﬃcient of 10% for our preliminary model
calculations in our study of the eastern terraced wadi at Horvat
Haluqim.
3.1. Average annual runoﬀcoeﬃcients measured in relation to
reconstructed ancient farms or cisterns
The only combined hydrological and agronomic research in the
Negev Highlands to investigate the functioning of ancient farming
systems based on runoﬀand ﬂoodwater was conducted by Evenari et al.
(1982). They restored in 1958 an ancient terraced wadi with hillside
conduits near the Byzantine town of Shivta (Fig. 1). A few years later, in
1960, they restored another ancient Byzantine farm near the town of
Avdat (Fig. 1). Both farming systems are characterised by a series of
hillside conduits, which collect runoﬀfrom the adjacent hillslopes
(Fig. 6).
Their hydrological investigations included detailed rainfall and
runoﬀ/ﬂoodwater measurements from 1960 to 1967, besides related
agronomic investigations that continued into the 1980s. Shanan es-
tablished an evaporation pan, 14 rain gauges to measure precipitation
amounts/intensities and 8 automatic hydrographs with V-notch weirs
(Fig. 6) to measure runoﬀvolumes and ﬂow rates at each outﬂow point
of a conduit channel or natural stream channel into the terraced agri-
cultural ﬁelds (Shanan, 1975, 2000; Shanan and Schick, 1980; Evenari
et al., 1982). The rather ingenious Hillside Conduit System was ap-
parently developed and built during the Byzantine period, probably in
conjunction with the growth of perennial grapevines and industrial
wine production (Rubin, 1991; Erez Edelson, 2004). Grapevines are
small trees that require more water than seasonal ﬁeld crops like wheat
and barley.
The extensive and systematic research by Shanan (Table 2) of runoﬀ
from various diﬀerent watershed sizes highlights the eﬀect of catch-
ment size on runoﬀcoeﬃcient (Table 2): the smaller the catchment
area, the larger the runoﬀcoeﬃcient (Shanan and Schick, 1980;
Shanan, 2000; Evenari et al., 1982).
Concerning the southern catchment of the Avdat Farm, ﬁve hillside
conduits (Fig. 6: conduits 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7) artiﬁcially subdivide the
eastern hillslopes into smaller sub-catchments. The eastern hillslopes at
the Avdat Farm have a considerable length of about 340 m–215 m,
measured from the nearby hilltops in the east (Fig. 6) to the terraced
ﬁelds or to the natural streambed in the southern valley. Rock outcrops
(chalk and limestone, mostly of the Eocene Horsha Formation) occa-
sionally appear along the upper slopes, but loess soil and stones (rock
fragments) usually cover the Horsha Formation along the upper, middle
and lower parts of the slopes. All loessial soils in the central Negev
region are covered by a crust, about 2–4 mm thick (Shanan and Schick,
1980; Evenari et al., 1982). The closely spaced conduit channels in the
middle part of the eastern hillslope considerably shortened the length of
slowly moving overland ﬂow, converting the runoﬀinto channel ﬂow.
Thus less runoﬀwater was lost on the long hillslopes, due to inﬁltration.
Consequently, more water, also from the upper and middle part of the
long slopes, could reach the terraced agricultural ﬁelds (Shanan, 1975,
2000; Shanan and Schick, 1980; Evenari et al., 1982).

3.2. Runoﬀcoeﬃcients measured at a slope section of the Haluqim
Anticline
Detailed hydro-geomorphological research was conducted by Yair
et al. (1980) along an instrumented slope-section of the Haluqim An-
ticline west of Kibbutz Sede Boqer. The objectives of their investigations
were clearly stated: “the study of spatial variations in rainfall, runoﬀand
erosion processes along slopes” (Yair et al., 1980:243). Ancient agri-
cultural terraced wadi ﬁelds were not included in their investigations
and data collection. The studied part of the hillslope covers an area of
11 325 m2 (1.1 ha), in which a network of 19 rain gauges was estab-
lished, as well as an evaporation pan, a number of volumetric water
meters, water level recorders and suspended sediment samplers.
The investigated slope section includes three geological formations
(Fig. 7) of the Turonian period (Arkin and Braun, 1965). The Nezer
Formation, composed of well-bedded hard limestone, makes up the
upper part of the hillslope and its geomorphic surface is characterised
by alternating strips of bedrock exposure and loess soil/stone cover.
The middle part of the hillslope is composed of the Shivta Formation,
showing a geomorphic surface of massive oolitic calcarenite limestone,
generally devoid of soil cover. The Drorim Formation, situated at the
lower part of the hillslope, consists of limestone, chalk and marl, but
bedrock outcrops are limited and the geomorphic surface is largely
composed of colluvial deposits of loess soil and stones (Yair et al., 1980;
Lavee and Yair, 1990).
Unlike the hydrological research by Shanan at the reconstructed
ancient farms near Shivta and Avdat, described above, the hydrological
research by Yair et al. was not focused on runoﬀyields by ancient
agricultural ﬁelds or cisterns. The hillslope section (Fig. 7) was divided
for runoﬀmeasurements in the following manner Yair et al. (1980):
“The study of the spatial variations in slope runoﬀis based on 10 contiguous
plots draining parallel strips of the entire experimental site. Three of these
plots numbered 2, 4 and 9 were subdivided into three subplots each: a long
one, extending from the divide to the slope base and the two adjoining ones
short, draining the upper or lower section of the slope respectively”. Slope
length of the studied plots varies from 55 to 76 m and slope gradient
from 12 to 29.5% (Lavee and Yair, 1990).
Average annual runoﬀcoeﬃcients of the studied slope sections on
the Haluqim Anticline were unfortunately not published. However,
individual runoﬀcoeﬃcients were presented of three speciﬁc rainfall
events. A medium type of rainstorm occurred during 25–27 December
1988 (Yair and Raz-Yassif, 2004). It gave 12.2 mm precipitation in the
sub-catchment drained by the Upper Channel and 13.7 mm precipita-
tion in the sub-catchment drained by the Lower Channel. The distance
between the hydrometric stations of the Upper and the Lower Channel
is 200 m.
Concerning the location and size of the sub-catchments, as well as
the position of the hydrometric stations, the authors write (Yair and
Raz-Yassif, 2004:157): “The ﬁrst (named Upper Channel) is located at the
transition from the headwater rocky area into the alluvial reach of a ﬁrst-
order drainage basin and drains 0.8 ha. The convergent slopes are short, and
very extensive rocky outcrops, almost devoid of soil and vegetation cover,
form most of the surface. The second (Lower Channel) is located at the
mouth of the same drainage basin and drains 2.1 ha. The valley side slopes
are long and soil cover is more extensive. It is characterised by soil strips at
the base of rock steps at the upper rocky slope sections and a colluvial mantle
at the base of long slopes”.
The geological formations, however, are not mentioned. It seems
that the Upper Channel drains only the Nezer and Shivta Formations,
while the Lower Channel drains also the colluvial slope overlying the
Drorim Formation. Anyhow, the runoﬀcoeﬃcient of the Upper Channel
is 28% and of the Lower Channel only 3.8% (Yair and Raz-Yassif,
2004:161). The authors concluded that most runoﬀproduced by the
Lower Channel sub-catchment rocky upper slope inﬁltrated into the
lower colluvial slope. Thus little runoﬀreached the hydrometric station
at the base of the colluvial slope, resulting in a runoﬀcoeﬃcient of
merely 3.8% in a catchment of only 2.1 ha, compared to 28% for the
hydrometric station at the base of the headwater rocky area of the slope
with a catchment of 0.8 ha.
An extensive regional rainstorm covered most of the Negev desert
during March 22–23, 1991. The event lasted for 36 h and consisted of
three major spells, (Yair and Kossovsky, 2002). The amount of pre-
cipitation was 45.6 mm, being about half of the average annual total in
the Haluqim – Sede Boqer area. A rainfall event of such magnitude is
rare and may occur once every 10 years. The runoﬀcoeﬃcients during
this event were 65% in the Upper Channel and 37% in the Lower
Channel (Yair and Kossovsky, 2002). Such a large rainstorm caused a
tenfold increase in the runoﬀcoeﬃcient at the base of the colluvial
slope (Lower Channel) and more than doubled the runoﬀcoeﬃcient for
the rocky upper slope (Upper Channel), as compared to the 13 mm
rainfall event of 25–27 December 1988.
The highest recorded rainfall episode occurred during January 1–3,
1992, which gave 53.2 mm of precipitation (Yair and Kossovsky, 2002).
Such a rainfall is truly exceptional and took place during the wettest
year ever recorded in Israel, 1991–92, since the beginning of pre-
cipitation measurements in the middle of the 19th century. The runoﬀ
coeﬃcient was 52.7% in the upper channel and 28% in the lower
channel (Yair and Kossovsky, 2002). These ﬁgures are slightly lower
than in the previous case, but in the same order of magnitude. Such
large rainfall events are indeed very rare in the region and cannot be
used as a standard in relation to runoﬀyields for ancient agricultural

3.3. Geotechnical runoﬀcoeﬃcients of bedrock sample blocks, as well as
the importance of crusted loess soils
Novel measurements to determine geotechnical runoﬀcoeﬃcients
of bedrock types in the central Negev region were carried out by Wieler
et al. (2016). These runoﬀcoeﬃcients were measured in the lab on
small bedrock samples (blocks), having a volume of 1000 cm3. It is clear
that the resulting runoﬀis from a very small surface area, as the bed-
rock blocks appear to be about 10 × 15 × 7 cm in size. Nevertheless the
results obtained by Wieler et al. (2016) give a useful parameter to
compare the inherent runoﬀcontributing capacity of various geological
formations present in the central Negev desert. The authors also made a
useful analysis with GIS of stream order in which ancient agricultural
ﬁelds are situated within an area of 160 km2 west of Kibbutz Sede Boker
(Wieler et al., 2016:157).
However, their approach to calculate runoﬀcoeﬃcients of the
various drainage basins, based only on the geological formations in-
volved, seems not realistic in relation to the ancient agricultural ﬁelds.
The authors did not include in their investigation the presence of loess
soil, which is the predominant and practically omnipresent feature of
the hilly landscape in the central Negev Highlands. The bedrock of
many geological formations in the catchments of ancient farming ﬁelds
is often not exposed but covered by loess soil, usually mixed with
stones, as shown for the Shivta Farm (Fig. 8). The geological substratum
of the Shivta Farm (Table 3), as indicated by the geological map of
Shivta (Sneh et al., 2011), does not necessarily reﬂect the type of the
actual geomorphic surface on which runoﬀdevelops. Therefore, runoﬀ
calculations only based on bedrock runoﬀpotential ignore a signiﬁcant
part of the geomorphic surface reality, i.e. bedrock covered by loess.
A second misunderstanding is stated by the authors as follows
(Wieler et al., 2016:156): “Runoﬀcoeﬃcient for the loessic soil was not
dealt with in this work since we simulated only light rains; runoﬀthresholds
for the loessic soil are higher than for bedrock (Yair, 1983), therefore, no
parameters were deﬁned for the loessic soil”. Their perception, citing Yair
(1983), that light rains do not produce runoﬀon loess soil is erroneous.
The extensive multi-year hydrological research by Shanan (1975) at the
reconstructed Avdat Farm showed beyond any doubt that light rains
above 3 mm do produce runoﬀon loess covered slopes, see also Shanan
and Schick (1980) and Evenari et al. (1982). The crust on the loess soil
absorbs about 2.5–3 mm of rainfall, but then the crust is saturated and,
if the rain continues, runoﬀwill suddenly appear as a shining ﬁlm of
water on the loess surface, subsequently ﬂowing down as runoﬀover-
land ﬂow. This process has been witnessed repeatedly by the ﬁrst au-
thor (Bruins), who has lived for more than three decades in the central
Negev Highlands.
The signiﬁcance of crusted loess soil in the region for ancient
agriculture is clearly written by Evenari et al. (1982:109): “… most of
the rainfall of the region falls in relatively light showers of 3 to 10 mm at a
time. Now the loess soils typical of this region … form a characteristic crust
when wet. This crust soon becomes impermeable to rain and therefore there
is runoﬀeven with light rains … It was this character of the loess soils that
enabled the ancient farmers to harvest water from the hillsides even under
these low-rainfall desert conditions”.
The loess soils in the region are derived from dust deposition, set-
tling like snow on the entire landscape surface during dust storms. The
phenomenon of dust storms was not limited to the Late Pleistocene but
continued also during the Holocene. Each year quite a number of dust
storms occur in the Negev desert (Oﬀer and Goossens, 2001), depositing
dust that becomes loessial (silt-loam) soil with a crust.
For example, concerning the Avdat Farm watershed, the geological
substratum is composed mainly of chalk of the Eocene Horsha
Formation (geotechnical runoﬀcoeﬃcient 48%, Wieler et al., 2016)
and only for a small part by limestone of the Eocene Matred Formation
(geotechnical runoﬀcoeﬃcient 87%, Wieler et al., 2016). We carried
out supervised land cover classiﬁcation for the Avdat Farm catchment,
using an orthophoto image from the Survey of Israel and Erdas Imagine.
The results show that only 3% of the watershed surface is composed of
bedrock outcrops, whilst 93% is covered by loess soil (partly mixed
with stones), and 4% is covered by vegetation. Therefore, using bedrock
runoﬀcoeﬃcients of the geological substratum as a basis for calculating
the runoﬀcoeﬃcient of a drainage basin (Wieler et al., 2016:157), but
ignoring the predominant loess cover is unrealistic.
Finally, estimating the runoﬀcoeﬃcient of an entire drainage basin
is certainly legitimate in itself. But such an approach is perhaps less
useful in relation to ancient agricultural ﬁelds situated in the
streambed. The 46 drainage basins involved in their study range in size
from 53 ha to 5428 ha (Wieler et al., 2016:157).
For comparison, the southern watershed of the Avdat Farm has a
size of 30 ha, but the sub-catchments with conduit channels range in
size from 1 to 7 ha (Shanan and Schick, 1980). The average annual
runoﬀcoeﬃcient of these smaller sub-catchments is in the range of
5.0–12.2% (Table 2). The large eastern watershed of the Avdat Farm
has a size of 345 ha with an average annual runoﬀcoeﬃcient of only
2.8%, as measured by Hydrograph 8 (Fig. 6).

4. GIS-based hydrological model of terraced Wadi ﬁelds at Horvat
Haluqim
4.1. Average annual runoﬀcoeﬃcient: approximation rational
Our rational for approximating an average annual runoﬀcoeﬃcient
of 10% for the terraced wadi ﬁelds at Horvat Haluqim is based on the
instrumented hydrological records of the Avdat Farm (Shanan and
Schick, 1980; Evenari et al., 1982; Shanan, 2000) and the Haluqim
slope section (Yair et al., 1980; Lavee and Yair, 1990; Yair and
Kossovsky, 2002; Yair and Raz-Yassif, 2004).
The eastern wadi at Horvat Haluqim is a 1st order stream channel
(Figs. 2 and 9), in which 13 ancient terraced ﬁelds can be observed,
according to the number of visible terrace wall remains (Fig. 4). It is a
rural archaeological site and neither the terrace walls nor the related
terraced ﬁelds have been restored. The geological substratum at Horvat
Haluqim is the Turonian Nezer Formation (Table 3), which also makes
up the upper part of the investigated Haluqim slope section, in-
vestigated by Yair et al. (1980). Alternating strips of bedded rock out-
crops and strips of loess soil mixed with stones characterize the hill-
slopes of the Nezer Formation, both at Horvat Haluqim (Fig. 9) and at
the instrumented upper slope section of the Haluqim Anticline (Fig. 7).
However, the Shivta and Drorim Formations, situated along the
middle and lower part of the latter slope section, are not exposed in the
eastern wadi catchment of Horvat Haluqim. Moreover, there is no col-
luvium at the lower hillslopes at Horvat Haluim, as hard limestone
bedrock outcrop layers (Nezer Formation) appear also at the bottom of

length of the studied instrumented slope sections at the Haluqim An-

similar as the slope length at Horvat Haluqim (40–80 m).
Therefore, the hillslopes at Horvat Haluqim are comparable with the
upper part of the instrumented slope section at the Haluqim Anticline

Concerning bedrock exposure of the Nezer Formation at the Horvat
Haluqim eastern watershed, measured along transects from the water
divide on the western hill spur to the water divide on the eastern hill
spur (Fig. 9), bedrock surface coverage was found to be in the range of
17–57% (Bruins and Ore, 2008). Using Erdas Imagine based supervised
land cover classiﬁcation, we determined for the Horvat Haluqim wa-
tersheds that on average 23% of the surface is composed of bedrock
outcrops, 71% is loess soil (often mixed with stones) overlying the
bedrock in alternating strips, while vegetation cover is 6%.
Concerning the watershed of the Avdat Farm, we applied the same
methodology of supervised land cover classiﬁcation using Erdas
Imagine. Our results show that bedrock surface coverage at the Avdat
Farm watershed is only 3%, loess soil coverage (partly mixed with
stones) is 93%, and vegetation cover is 4%. These ﬁgures underline the
important contribution of loess covered areas in runoﬀproduction, as
shown by the extensive and long-term hydrological measurements by
Shanan. The crust on the loess makes it, under wet conditions, after
absorbing 2–3 mm of rainfall, rather impermeable, thus producing
signiﬁcant amounts of runoﬀ(Shanan and Schick, 1980; Evenari et al.,
1982; Shanan, 2000).
The hillslope length at Horvat Haluqim ranges from ∼40 to 80 m,
which is much shorter than hillslopes at the southern watershed of the
Avdat Farm. Concerning watershed size, the various conduit channels
at the Avdat Farm drain watersheds ranging in size from 1.0 to 7.0 ha,
being about 10–20 times larger than the watersheds (0.10–0.36 ha) of
the individual terraced ﬁelds at Horvat Haluqim (Table 4). The average
annual runoﬀcoeﬃcients of the above hillslope conduit catchments at
the Avdat Farm range between 5% and 12.2% (Table 2). The very small
runoﬀplots of 80 m2 at the Avdat Farm, having a slope length of 20 m,
have an average annual runoﬀcoeﬃcient of 25.4%.
Considering all the hydrological measurements and data at the
Avdat Farm and at the instrumented slope section of the Haluqim
Anticline, an average annual runoﬀcoeﬃcient of 10% for the hillslope
catchments of the individual terraced ﬁelds at Horvat Haluqim seems a
reasonable approximation, perhaps even too conservative.
The resulting runoﬀcalculations of our model (Table 4) are based
on precise determination of the catchment size of each individual ter-
raced ﬁeld, on the annual precipitation for each of three diﬀerent
rainfall years (an average rainfall year, 1989–90; a very wet year,
1991–92; a severe drought year, 1999–2000), and the approximated
average annual runoﬀcoeﬃcient of 10%. Rainfall data are from the
nearby meteorological station of the Israel Meteorological Service at
Kibbutz Sede Boker (Fig. 2), at a distance of just about 1700 m from
Horvat Haluqim.
4.2. Model calculated runoﬀyields during an average rainfall year, 1989-
90
Rainfall during the year 1989–90 totalled 88 mm, which can be
regarded as an average rainfall year, slightly below the long-term
average of 98 mm at Kibbutz Sede Boker during the period 1970–2002
(Kaﬂe and Bruins, 2009). Using a conservative average annual runoﬀ
coeﬃcient of 10%, our model calculated runoﬀamounts received by
the individual terraced ﬁelds, range from 119 to 232 mm (Table 4).
Hence there are considerable diﬀerences between the respective 13
terraced ﬁelds in terms of runoﬀyields, as indicated by the model.
The direct rainfall of 88 mm is added to the runoﬀyields in the
subsequent column (Table 4), to illustrate the total water amount re-
ceived by each terraced ﬁeld. Water quantities in the range of
200–300 mm were received by 9 of the 13 terraced ﬁelds in the eastern
wadi (Fig. 11). The two ﬁelds, situated most upstream, obtained more
water, in the range of 300–400 mm during an average rainfall year
(Fig. 11).
Considering the potential performance of annual ﬁeld crops with
the combined water amounts of both rainfall and runoﬀ, ranging from
207 to 365 mm during the rainy season, both barley and wheat may be
grown successfully. Concerning perennial fruit trees, grapevines may
suﬃce with about 350 mm of rainfall, which may be successful in some
of the terraced ﬁelds. Perhaps the average annual runoﬀcoeﬃcient of
10%, used for the model calculations, has been too conservative, be-
cause trees are grown successfully by the Jewish National Fund in
modern terraced wadi ﬁelds near Horvat Haluqim, as presented below
in section 5.

4.4. Model calculated runoﬀyields during a severe drought year

The amount of annual rainfall in the area was only 34 mm during
this harsh drought year. Calculated runoﬀamounts received by the
individual terraced ﬁelds range from 46 to 108 mm (Table 4). Adding in

whether perennial trees can survive such severe drought years? The
next section unmistakably proves that trees do survive drought years in
nearby modern terraced wadi ﬁelds, similar to those at Horvat Ha-

5. Trees in the otherwise tree-less desert
Wadis of 1st stream order on the Haluqim Anticline were terraced
by the Jewish National Fund some 1–2 km north-west of Horvat
Haluqim along Road 40, around the year 2000 or slightly afterwards.
These wadis had not been terraced in the past. Hence, there was no
legal problem (Antiquities Law) to build modern terrace walls (Figs. 3
and 14) to facilitate tree growth.
The natural landscape surface is characterised, like at Horvat
Haluqim, by bedded limestone of the Nezer Formation, partly covered
by crusted loess soil and stones. The modern stone terrace walls cap-
tured runoﬀwater (Figs. 3 and 14) from these geomorphic surfaces
during rainfall events and trees were established successfully in the
following years (Fig. 15). It is clear that in the period of about 14 years
of tree growth, captured by Figs. 14 and 15, also drought years oc-
curred. Statistically a drought year in Israel can be expected on average
once every three years (Bruins, 2000).
Therefore, the trees may receive appreciable runoﬀwater amounts
even during drought years. Their survival may also relate to runoﬀ
water from previous wetter years. Such water may be held by capillary
force for considerable time in the deeper loessial subsoil. Moreover, the
reduction of water loss by evaporation was found to be related to the
sealing properties of the crust that covers loess soils in the Negev (Sela
et al., 2012). A model for seal hydraulic properties studied spatial
variations of water content over an entire loess hillslope in the northern
Negev (near Lehavim) in relation to the sealing eﬀect of the surface
crust (Sela et al., 2012).
The ancient Shivta Farm (Fig. 8), reconstructed by Evenari, Shanan
and Tadmor in 1958, still shows many surviving fruit trees, including
olive, pomegranate, ﬁg, grapevine and carob. Obviously, these fruit
trees have managed to survive many drought years, including one of the
worst periods, 1998–2000, when a severe drought lasted for two con-
secutive years. Both the joint eﬀect of soil texture of loess soils (usually
silt-loam), having excellent water-holding properties, and the surface
crust that reduces evaporation from the soil, serve to mitigate the eﬀect
of drought years.

Tadmor in 1960, agriculture started in the 1960–61 rainfall year.

6. Final discussion and conclusions
Our approach, using a GIS-based hydrological model, opens an en-
tirely new avenue to study ancient agricultural systems in the central
Negev desert, because each and every terraced ﬁeld can be investigated
in a non-invasive manner. The availability of high resolution LiDAR
data and detailed orthophoto images enables the generation of detailed
DEMs and classiﬁcation of land covers. These components constitute
the infrastructure for accurate spatial calculations of boundaries and
size assessments of each catchment area that contributes runoﬀto a
speciﬁc ancient agricultural terraced ﬁeld and cistern. The model is also
suited for modern applications to develop rainwater harvesting pro-
jects.
However, more research is required to establish applicable rules to
estimate more precisely the runoﬀcoeﬃcients that ought to be used in
case-sensitive model calculations. More research is also required to test
the model against hydrological data measured with conventional hy-
drographs and other instrumented hydrological equipment.
Following the detailed investigations by Yair and his colleagues of
an instrumented hillslope at the Haluqim Anticline, there has been a
tendency in some of the literature to overemphasize the signiﬁcance of
bedrock surfaces in runoﬀproduction. The systematic and extensive
hydrological results of the Avdat Farm (Shanan and Schick, 1980;
Evenari et al., 1982; Shanan, 2000) should not be ignored. These results
clearly show that also crusted loess soil surfaces, which clearly dom-
inate in areal extent over clean bedrock surfaces in the Negev High-
lands, can produce signiﬁcant amounts of runoﬀ.
The apparent lack of terraced wadi ﬁelds with stone terrace walls in
the loess region north of the central Negev Highlands, as noted by Yair
(1983), seems not to be related to a lack of runoﬀpotential but is
probably caused by other factors. First, the lack of hard bedrock out-
crops in the northern Negev makes it very costly to quarry and move
from afar limestone building stones to make stone terrace walls in the
wadi beds. Mudbricks were often used to build houses in areas with
loess or alluvial sediments. However, mudbricks are not suitable to
build terrace walls in wadi beds to withstand runoﬀand ﬂoodwater
ﬂows. Eocene chalk does occur below the extensive loess cover in this
region, but even chalk is not used for making stone terrace walls.
Second, the geomorphology in this region of the northern Negev shows
many examples of V-shaped valleys which are too narrow in the wadi
bed to facilitate enough space for agricultural ﬁelds.
Nevertheless, some ancient agricultural ﬁelds and ancient farm
buildings were discovered during archaeological surveys (Map 132) in
the Nahal Beqa area (Baumgarten, personal communication, 2011;
Bruins, 2012:32). Bedouin living in the area today use bulldozers to
make terrace walls of soil in suitable valleys to capture runoﬀfrom
loess-covered catchments to sustain fruit trees, particularly olives.
Whether used in typical loess areas or in areas with both bedrock
exposures and loess-covered surfaces, the critical issue for success of the
GIS-based hydrological model is the correct approximation of the runoﬀ
coeﬃcient in each particular case.
